scenes.reply:
I couldn’t verify the exact sentence within the portion you’ve read, so I don’t want to invent or misquote it.

On the role itself: “manager” can feel awkward because saying it makes a change sound settled before it feels settled inside you. The title may be accurate while still feeling borrowed, oversized, or unlike your usual way of describing yourself. Sometimes the awkwardness is simply the lag between taking on a role and inhabiting it.

You might try saying it in lower-stakes forms—“I’m managing this project,” or “I’m learning to be a manager”—and notice which version feels more truthful. What part feels most awkward: the word itself, the authority it implies, or the fear that others will expect you to already know how to do it?

scenes.input_line: I still stumble over calling myself a manager. At today's team introduction I nearly said designer again, even though I like the new work. Could we think about why naming a new role feels so awkward, and find an introduction that feels honest to me?
scenes.reply:
That awkwardness makes sense: a role change can be real before it feels familiar in your own voice. “Designer” may still be part of your story, while “manager” names what you’re doing now—not everything you are.

You could try an introduction that bridges the two:

- “I’m [Name], and I recently moved from design into management. I’m enjoying helping the team do its best work.”
- “I’m [Name]. My background is in design, and I’m now managing the team.”
- “I’m [Name], the team’s manager. I came from a design background, so I’m especially interested in how we make good work together.”

The first may feel most honest if you’re still growing into the title: it doesn’t force you to pretend the transition is complete emotionally. You could also practice saying it privately a few times—not to convince yourself, but to let the words become less surprising. Which part feels truest: naming the transition, naming your design background, or naming what you hope to contribute as a manager?
